scenes.visual: Title card 'Paying to Go Uphill' over the same grey-and-cream membrane as the first film, a yellow ATP token resting on it. Same world and COLOUR MAP as the first film: THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene, both films and the lesson's take-homes: WATER molecules = small BLUE dots; SODIUM ions = ORANGE dots labelled 'Na+'; CHLORIDE ions = GREEN dots labelled 'Cl-'; POTASSIUM ions = PURPLE dots labelled 'K+'; ATP = YELLOW token; OXYGEN = small WHITE dots with a grey outline; DYE = RED dots; MEMBRANE = two rows of GREY round heads with PALE cream tails meeting in the middle; PROTEINS in the membrane = TEAL blocks. A small counter box sits top right in every scene. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: In the first film, whatever could cross ran downhill for free. So how does a cell keep so much sodium outside, and so much potassium inside?
scenes.visual: Quick replay thumbnail of the two tanks with the end-card line, then it shrinks away. The membrane fills the screen with 'OUTSIDE the cell' above and 'INSIDE the cell' below; orange and purple dots appear with a question mark.
scenes.narration: In the first film, whatever could cross ran downhill for free. So how does a cell keep so much sodium outside, and so much potassium inside?

scenes.tts: Look at an animal cell's membrane. Sodium, shown in orange, is much higher outside the cell. Potassium, shown in purple, is much higher inside. Each ion sits at the top of its own hill.
scenes.caption: Look at an animal cell's membrane. Sodium (Na+), shown in orange, is much higher outside the cell. Potassium (K+), shown in purple, is much higher inside. Each ion sits at the top of its own hill.
scenes.visual: Two bar meters at the side: orange Na+ bar tall outside, short inside; purple K+ bar tall inside, short outside (schematic heights). Many orange dots above the membrane, many purple dots below.
scenes.narration: Look at an animal cell's membrane. Sodium (Na+), shown in orange, is much higher outside the cell. Potassium (K+), shown in purple, is much higher inside. Each ion sits at the top of its own hill.

scenes.tts: A few channels in the membrane leak. Sodium trickles in, and potassium trickles out. Each ion runs downhill, and the two differences start to shrink.
scenes.visual: Two teal leak channels open. Orange dots drip downward through one, purple dots drip upward through the other. The meter bars slowly creep toward each other (schematic).
scenes.narration: A few channels in the membrane leak. Sodium trickles in, and potassium trickles out. Each ion runs downhill, and the two differences start to shrink.

scenes.tts: A leak channel is an open tunnel, so ions pass through it only downhill. For ions, the hill also depends on the membrane's voltage. Biology Two covers that part. A pump is different. It grabs ions, changes shape, and spends energy to carry them uphill.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, a teal open tunnel with dots flowing downhill only, labelled 'channel: downhill only'. Right, a larger teal block with a pocket, labelled 'pump: grabs, changes shape, spends energy'.
scenes.caption: A leak channel is an open tunnel, so ions pass through it only downhill. For ions, the hill also depends on the membrane's voltage. Biology II covers that part. A pump is different. It grabs ions, changes shape, and spends energy to carry them uphill.
scenes.narration: A leak channel is an open tunnel, so ions pass through it only downhill. For ions, the hill also depends on the membrane's voltage. Biology II covers that part. A pump is different. It grabs ions, changes shape, and spends energy to carry them uphill.

scenes.tts: Watch one cycle of the sodium-potassium pump. First, three sodium ions bind to the pump on the inside of the cell.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the pump block spanning the membrane, pocket open to the inside. Three orange Na+ dots slot into the pocket one by one. Counter box rows: 'ATP spent 0', 'Na+ out 0', 'K+ in 0'.
scenes.narration: Watch one cycle of the sodium-potassium pump. First, three sodium ions bind to the pump on the inside of the cell.

scenes.tts: The pump spends one A T P, the molecule that carries usable energy around the cell. The pump changes shape and releases the three sodium ions outside.
scenes.visual: A yellow ATP token docks on the inner face and fades with a small flash. The block twists so the pocket opens outward; the three orange dots pop out above. Counters: 'ATP spent 1', 'Na+ out 3'.
scenes.caption: The pump spends one ATP, the molecule that carries usable energy around the cell. The pump changes shape and releases the three sodium ions outside.
scenes.narration: The pump spends one ATP, the molecule that carries usable energy around the cell. The pump changes shape and releases the three sodium ions outside.

scenes.tts: Now two potassium ions bind on the outside. The pump changes shape again and carries them in. Both trips went uphill, against each ion's gradient.
scenes.visual: Two purple K+ dots slot into the outward-facing pocket; the block twists back and releases them below. Counter: 'K+ in 2'. Small uphill ramp icons flash beside each ion type.
scenes.narration: Now two potassium ions bind on the outside. The pump changes shape again and carries them in. Both trips went uphill, against each ion's gradient.

scenes.tts: Every cycle, one A T P spent, three sodium out, two potassium in. While the pump keeps running, the meters hold steady, even though the leaks never close.
scenes.visual: The cycle repeats at speed; counters climb together in the ratio shown on screen as '1 ATP : 3 Na+ out : 2 K+ in'. Leak channels still dripping; meter bars hold at their uneven heights.
scenes.caption: Every cycle, one ATP spent, three sodium out, two potassium in. While the pump keeps running, the meters hold steady, even though the leaks never close.
scenes.narration: Every cycle, one ATP spent, three sodium out, two potassium in. While the pump keeps running, the meters hold steady, even though the leaks never close.

scenes.tts: Movement that uses the cell's energy, often from A T P, is active transport. It can move a substance against its gradient. Diffusion and osmosis are passive transport, and need no energy from the cell.
scenes.visual: Two labelled columns appear: 'ACTIVE TRANSPORT: uses energy, often ATP; can go uphill' with the pump and a yellow token; 'PASSIVE TRANSPORT: no energy from the cell; downhill' with dye, water and a leak channel.
scenes.caption: Movement that uses the cell's energy, often from ATP, is active transport. It can move a substance against its gradient. Diffusion and osmosis are passive transport, and need no energy from the cell.
scenes.narration: Movement that uses the cell's energy, often from ATP, is active transport. It can move a substance against its gradient. Diffusion and osmosis are passive transport, and need no energy from the cell.

scenes.tts: Now the cell runs out of A T P. The leak channels stay open. Which way will sodium move now? And which way will potassium move? Pause and predict.
scenes.visual: The yellow token supply bin empties, labelled 'ATP: none left'. Pause card 'Pause and predict' with arrows and question marks beside the orange and purple meters.
scenes.caption: Now the cell runs out of ATP. The leak channels stay open. Which way will sodium move now? And which way will potassium move? Pause and predict.
scenes.narration: Now the cell runs out of ATP. The leak channels stay open. Which way will sodium move now? And which way will potassium move? Pause and predict.

scenes.visual: Pause card holds; pump block still.

scenes.tts: The pump freezes. Sodium leaks in and potassium leaks out, both downhill. The two differences slowly shrink. The first film's rule has taken over again.
scenes.visual: Pump block greys out. Orange dots stream down through a leak, purple dots stream up. Both meter bars move toward each other; label 'differences shrinking (schematic)', with no claim that they reach equal. A small inset of the first film's downhill ramp appears.
scenes.narration: The pump freezes. Sodium leaks in and potassium leaks out, both downhill. The two differences slowly shrink. The first film's rule has taken over again.

scenes.tts: So holding a difference is not a one-time payment. The leaks undo the pump's work all the time. The pump must keep spending A T P, cycle after cycle. Stop paying, and the differences drain away.
scenes.visual: Restart: a new yellow token supply arrives, the pump turns again, and the meters climb back apart. Counter 'ATP spent' keeps ticking up while leak channels keep dripping.
scenes.caption: So holding a difference is not a one-time payment. The leaks undo the pump's work all the time. The pump must keep spending ATP, cycle after cycle. Stop paying, and the differences drain away.
scenes.narration: So holding a difference is not a one-time payment. The leaks undo the pump's work all the time. The pump must keep spending ATP, cycle after cycle. Stop paying, and the differences drain away.

scenes.tts: That gives you one test for a substance crossing on its own. Is it going downhill? Then it is passive and free. Is it going uphill? Then the cell is paying.
scenes.visual: Two ramps side by side: downhill ramp with a ball rolling, labelled 'crossing on its own, downhill: passive, free'; uphill ramp with a ball pushed up beside a yellow ATP token, labelled 'uphill: the cell pays'.
scenes.narration: That gives you one test for a substance crossing on its own. Is it going downhill? Then it is passive and free. Is it going uphill? Then the cell is paying.

scenes.visual: End card, Hex mascot beside the line: 'Downhill is free; uphill costs energy, every cycle.'
